newsitem.title: ITALY: New Alitalia operation takes wing.
newsitem.headline: New Alitalia operation takes wing.

text.p: Italian state carrier Alitalia launched a new operating division on Thursday in a restructuring plan to speed the ailing airline back to profit.
The wholly-owned company, called Alitalia Team, will drastically cut labour costs and is expected to absorb all the airline's passenger operations by the end of the century.

"Alitalia is now on the attack again. We are not a wounded elephant which can be battered from all sides," managing director Domenico Cempella told a news conference in a cavernous aircraft hangar at Rome's Fiumicino airport.
But Cempella acknowledged that the task of turning the group back into the black after eight successive years of losses would not be easy.

"There is still an awful lot to do to resolve our problems," Cempella said, confirming that the group was flying towards losses of 1.2 trillion lire ($790 million) in 1996, largely because of 800 billion lire of restructuring costs.

However he said ticket sales had increased by 10 percent in the first 10 months of the year, while capacity had risen nine percent. He said the group was ready to lower fares across the board and forecast a profit of 170 billion for 1997.
"We have decided we have to lower costs and improve service...Alitalia Team represents a strong symbol of how we are changing," he said.

The new division, dubbed a Highly Competitive Carrier, will start with a fleet of 22 aircraft, growing to 33 by the end of April 1997. With newly negotiated contracts, cabin crew labour costs for the unit will be cut by 25 percent.
Pilot costs throughout the company will also gradually become more competitive, an Alitalia official said.
Alitalia management were locked in bitter conflict with unions for more than a year over plans to slash hefty personnel costs and boost productivity.

A truce was finally called last June when labour leaders agreed to a rescue package which allowed for between 20-30 percent of the group's shares to be reserved for employees after the firm's recapitalisation and privatisation.
Under the terms of the rescue plan, the airline called for a three trillion lire capital increase, with the government promising to provide much of the new cash.
The European Commission in Brussels has still not given clearance for the injection of state aid and Cempella said Alitalia was waiting for the bulk of the fresh funds.
In the meantime the company would push ahead with its 38-point restructuring plan, he said, which envisages Alitalia staffing numbers falling to 13,000 by the year 2000 from over 16,000 at present.
Over the same period, the company hoped to increase its fleet of aircraft from some 180 to around 200, Alitalia Team director general Franco Giudice said.
He added that debt-laden Alitalia would enhance its code-sharing scheme with U.S. airline Continental, but said talk of any strategic alliances or cross-share holdings in the sector were premature.

"At the moment Alitalia's economic situation prevents it from buying a stake in another airline while Alitalia itself is not a present an appetising prospect for other firms," he said. $1 + 1,516 lire
